title: Expectations, outcomes, and challenges of modern code review
rationale_md:
# T2-B01 — Bacchelli & Bird (2013), "Expectations, outcomes, and challenges of modern code review"

**Status:** Marked for Track 2 inclusion (2026-09-02). Not yet written to `01b_identification_track2_anchors.csv`.

## Bibliographic entry

Bacchelli, A., & Bird, C. (2013). Expectations, outcomes, and challenges of modern code review. *Proceedings of the 2013 International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE)*, 712-721. IEEE.

**DOI:** `10.1109/ICSE.2013.6606617`

## Quality signals (retrieved 2026-09-02)

| Signal | Value |
|---|---|
| Semantic Scholar total citations | 876 |
| Semantic Scholar influential citations | 136 |
| Venue | ICSE 2013 (International Conference on Software Engineering) |
| Venue tier | CORE A* (top-tier SE conference) |
| SJR quartile | n/a (conference; SJR indexes journals) |

## Why it matters for the correctness wedge

This is the paper that coined and empirically characterised "modern code review" (MCR) as distinct from Fagan-style formal inspection: lightweight, tool-based, asynchronous, motivated by knowledge transfer and defect-finding. Every subsequent MCR paper cites it. The core empirical finding is that developers' stated expectation (find defects) diverges from observed outcomes (knowledge transfer, code improvement, alternative solutions). That gap is exactly the wedge the thesis is built on: reviewers do not reliably catch correctness defects, so any productivity boost from Copilot that shifts defect burden onto review is undertheorised.

## Fit vs Ch2 sections

- Anchors the "what MCR actually does" paragraph in the code-review foundations section.
- Provides the empirical grounding for the correctness-versus-throughput wedge. Bacchelli and Bird found that reviewers themselves report that defect-finding is not the primary observed outcome.
- Cited by essentially every downstream MCR study (McIntosh 2016, Sadowski 2018, plus Rigby 2012 predecessor work), so leaving it out would be a defensibility problem at viva.

## Track 2 categorisation (proposed)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| `anchor_id` | `T2-B01` |
| `category` | `code_review_foundations` |
| `register` | `recommended_addition` |
| `source_method` | `purposive_selection` |
| `discovery_provenance` | Canonical MCR foundational reference; cited by every downstream MCR study encountered during the pivot-doc review |
| `target_chapter` | Ch2 (code-review foundations / correctness wedge subsection) |

## Research unit and screening

| Screen | Value |
|---|---|
| `research_unit` | `developer` |
| `unit_alignment` | `mismatch` |
| `psychology_adjacent` | `no` |

**Note.** Developer-level (17 Microsoft interviews). Use for MCR construct definition only; do not extend developer-perception claims to repository-level defect outcomes.

## Decision rationale

The signal strength is exceptional (876 total, 136 influential citations for a conference paper is elite tier) and the venue (ICSE) is the top-tier SE conference. Combined with the paper's role as the canonical MCR reference, the risk of not including it is higher than any risk of including it. The reference is a defensible, non-negotiable anchor for the correctness wedge.

**Decision:** Include in Track 2.

# T2-B02 — Sadowski, Söderberg, Church, Sipko & Bacchelli (2018), "Modern code review: A case study at Google"

**Status:** Marked for Track 2 inclusion (2026-09-02). Not yet written to `01b_identification_track2_anchors.csv`.

## Bibliographic entry

Sadowski, C., Söderberg, E., Church, L., Sipko, M., & Bacchelli, A. (2018). Modern code review: A case study at Google. *Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Software Engineering: Software Engineering in Practice (ICSE-SEIP '18)*, 181-190. ACM.

**DOI:** `10.1145/3183519.3183525`

## Quality signals (retrieved 2026-09-02)

| Signal | Value |
|---|---|
| Semantic Scholar total citations | 381 |
| Semantic Scholar influential citations | 44 |
| Venue | ICSE-SEIP 2018 (Software Engineering in Practice track) |
| Venue tier | CORE A* (ICSE main-conference host) |
| SJR quartile | n/a (conference; SJR indexes journals) |

## Why it matters for the correctness wedge

Sadowski et al. is the industrial-scale companion to Bacchelli and Bird 2013. Where Bacchelli and Bird interviewed 17 Microsoft developers, Sadowski et al. describe how code review actually runs at Google, across thousands of engineers doing millions of reviews per year. The empirical spine of the paper: Google's stated motivation for code review is education and code base health, not defect detection, and the median review is small, fast, and reviewed by one person. That inverts the classical Fagan inspection model completely, and it is exactly the kind of primary-source industrial evidence that a viva panel expects when a candidate claims MCR has drifted away from correctness enforcement. Sadowski and Bacchelli overlap on authorship, which reinforces continuity with B1's construct.

## Fit vs Ch2 sections

- Anchors the industrial-scale MCR paragraph as evidence that the correctness wedge is not an artefact of small-shop practice; it survives at hyperscale.
- Justifies the claim that MCR's observed function is knowledge propagation and codebase discipline, which is the specific mechanism that Copilot destabilises when review must now cover machine-suggested code.
- Managerial-implication register: the paper is quotable to a practising manager because Google is a recognisable authority; the wedge is defensible to a non-academic reader.

|---|---|

| `unit_alignment` | `aligned` |
| `psychology_adjacent` | `no` |

**Note.** Google-wide MCR system; organizational proxy for corporate-sponsored OSS setting.

## Decision rationale

The citation signal (381 total, 44 influential) is strong for an eight-year-old SEIP industry-track paper and the venue is the top-tier SE conference host. More importantly, the evidence type is complementary to B1: B1 gives the construct, B2 gives the hyperscale confirmation. Together they neutralise the "your wedge is only true at small companies" viva line. Omitting B2 would leave a defensibility gap the panel is trained to exploit.

**Decision:** Include in Track 2.

title: An empirical study of the impact of modern code review practices on software quality
rationale_md:
# T2-B03 — McIntosh, Kamei, Adams & Hassan (2016), "An empirical study of the impact of modern code review practices on software quality"

**Status:** Marked for Track 2 inclusion (2026-09-02). Not yet written to `01b_identification_track2_anchors.csv`.

## Bibliographic entry

McIntosh, S., Kamei, Y., Adams, B., & Hassan, A. E. (2016). An empirical study of the impact of modern code review practices on software quality. *Empirical Software Engineering*, *21*(5), 2146-2189. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10664-015-9381-9

**DOI:** `10.1007/s10664-015-9381-9`

## Quality signals (retrieved 2026-09-02)

| Signal | Value |
|---|---|
| Semantic Scholar total citations | 364 |
| Semantic Scholar influential citations | 26 |
| Venue | Empirical Software Engineering (Springer) |
| Venue tier | Top empirical-SE journal |
| SJR quartile | Q1 |

## Why it matters for the correctness wedge

This is the paper that turned the MCR-versus-quality question into a quantitative empirical claim rather than a descriptive one. McIntosh et al. mined the review histories of Qt, VTK, and ITK (three large FOSS projects with full public review records) and modelled post-release defect density as a function of review coverage, participation, and reviewer experience. The finding: components with low review coverage or low reviewer expertise show significantly higher post-release defect density, while superficial review (fast, unengaged) does not help. That is the quantitative form of the correctness wedge: reviewers in observed practice do act as a partial defect-catching layer, but effectiveness is bounded by reviewer capacity, and Copilot pushes more machine-generated code through that same bounded capacity.

## Fit vs Ch2 sections

- Quantitatively anchors the "reviewers as a bounded defect-catching layer" argument. B1 and B2 give the qualitative and hyperscale-descriptive frame; B3 supplies the econometric spine.
- Direct precedent for the thesis outcome variable (post-release defect density) and for treating reviewer experience as a moderator.
- Adams and Hassan are among the most cited MSR (mining software repositories) authors, so the paper's provenance is well recognised in the empirical-SE community that the viva panel will invoke.
- EMSE is Q1, so the paper carries journal-level weight that B1 and B2 lack.

## Track 2 categorisation (proposed)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| `anchor_id` | `T2-B03` |
| `category` | `code_review_foundations` |
| `register` | `recommended_addition` |
| `source_method` | `purposive_selection` |
| `discovery_provenance` | Canonical empirical-MCR quality-outcome study; cited in essentially every subsequent quantitative MCR paper |
| `target_chapter` | Ch2 (code-review foundations / correctness wedge subsection) |

## Research unit and screening

| Screen | Value |
|---|---|
| `research_unit` | `repository` |
| `unit_alignment` | `aligned` |
| `psychology_adjacent` | `no` |

**Note.** Repository-level defect models on Qt, VTK, ITK (file/component-level).

## Decision rationale

This is the strongest single reference in Block B for the thesis' quantitative argument. The journal signal (Q1 EMSE) combined with 364 citations and a direct quantitative link to defect outcomes makes it an obligatory anchor. Omitting it would leave the reader asking "where is the empirical evidence for your quality claim?" — a viva-lethal question.

**Decision:** Include in Track 2.

# T2-B04 — Rigby & Bird (2013), "Convergent contemporary software peer review practices"

**Status:** Marked for Track 2 inclusion (2026-09-02). Not yet written to `01b_identification_track2_anchors.csv`.

## Bibliographic entry

Rigby, P. C., & Bird, C. (2013). Convergent contemporary software peer review practices. *Proceedings of the 2013 9th Joint Meeting on Foundations of Software Engineering (ESEC/FSE 2013)*, 202-212. ACM.

**DOI:** `10.1145/2491411.2491444`

## Quality signals (retrieved 2026-09-02)

| Signal | Value |
|---|---|
| Semantic Scholar total citations | 374 |
| Semantic Scholar influential citations | 32 |
| Venue | ESEC/FSE 2013 (joint European Software Engineering Conference and ACM SIGSOFT Symposium on the Foundations of Software Engineering) |
| Venue tier | CORE A* (joint top-tier SE conference) |
| SJR quartile | n/a (conference; SJR indexes journals) |

## Why it matters for the correctness wedge

Rigby and Bird compare MCR practices across five organisations, Microsoft, Google, AMD, Bing, and OSS projects, and show that MCR converges on a common shape regardless of organisational type: small change sets, few reviewers, fast turnaround, informal discussion, and defect-finding as a stated but not dominant observed motivation. This is the cross-organisational convergence evidence that neutralises the viva line "your wedge is a Microsoft-only or Google-only artefact". B1 gave the construct with 17 Microsoft developers, B2 gave hyperscale confirmation at Google, B4 gives cross-organisational convergence. Together they lock the wedge as structural to MCR, not incidental to one shop.

## Fit vs Ch2 sections

- Anchors the "cross-organisational convergence of MCR practice" paragraph in the code-review foundations section.
- Blocks the viva line that the correctness wedge is confined to one organisation or one culture.
- Managerial-implication register: the paper is quotable to a practising manager because it names five recognisable organisations and reports a common pattern, which reads as robust generalisation rather than case-study speculation.

| `target_chapter` | Ch2 (code-review foundations / correctness wedge subsection) |

## Research unit and screening

| Screen | Value |
|---|---|
| `research_unit` | `organization` |
| `unit_alignment` | `aligned` |
| `psychology_adjacent` | `no` |

**Note.** Cross-organisational comparison (Microsoft, Google, AMD, Bing, OSS).

## Decision rationale

The citation signal (374 total, 32 influential) matches B1 in magnitude and the venue (ESEC/FSE) is a joint top-tier SE conference. The distinct contribution over B1 and B2 is cross-organisational convergence: the paper's argument that MCR looks the same at Microsoft, Google, AMD, Bing, and in OSS is the exact evidence needed to defend the correctness wedge as structural rather than local. Omitting B4 would leave that generalisation unsupported.

**Decision:** Include in Track 2.

title: What improves developer productivity at Google? Code quality
rationale_md:
# T2-B06 — Cheng, Rios, Nagappan & Zimmermann (2022), "What improves developer productivity at Google? Code quality"

**Status:** Marked for Track 2 inclusion (2026-09-02). Not yet written to `01b_identification_track2_anchors.csv`.

## Bibliographic entry

Cheng, L., Rios, M., Nagappan, N., & Zimmermann, T. (2022). What improves developer productivity at Google? Code quality. *Proceedings of the 30th ACM Joint European Software Engineering Conference and Symposium on the Foundations of Software Engineering (ESEC/FSE 2022)*, 1302-1313. ACM.

**DOI:** `10.1145/3540250.3558940`

## Quality signals (retrieved 2026-09-02)

| Signal | Value |
|---|---|
| Semantic Scholar total citations | 29 |
| Semantic Scholar influential citations | 1 |
| Venue | ESEC/FSE 2022 (joint European Software Engineering Conference and ACM SIGSOFT Symposium on the Foundations of Software Engineering) |
| Venue tier | CORE A* |
| SJR quartile | n/a (conference; SJR indexes journals) |

## Why it matters for the correctness wedge

Cheng et al. use survey and log data from Google engineers to test what actually correlates with self-reported productivity, and the headline finding is that code quality is the single strongest correlate: engineers report higher productivity in high-quality codebases and lower productivity in low-quality ones. That is the quality-discount wedge stated in reverse: if quality raises productivity, then productivity gains that erode quality are not productivity gains at steady state. For a thesis whose Chapter 3 estimand is the quality-discounted productivity contrast, this paper is the direct motivation reference: Google, self-reported evidence, empirical, current-generation.

## Fit vs Ch2 sections

- Anchors the "quality-productivity coupling" paragraph, which is the direct motivation for the quality-discount wedge in Chapter 3.
- Provides the industrial-side empirical statement that quality is a productivity input, not a downstream QA concern. The thesis inverts this framing to argue that Copilot's productivity claim must be net of quality change.
- Best-available current source: no other paper states the quality-as-productivity-input finding this cleanly at industrial scale in the AI-code era.

## Track 2 categorisation (proposed)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| `anchor_id` | `T2-B06` |
| `category` | `quality_productivity_coupling` (new slug; distinguishes the wedge-motivation cluster from the code-review-foundations cluster) |
| `register` | `recommended_addition` |
| `source_method` | `purposive_selection` |
| `discovery_provenance` | Pivot-doc candidate; motivates the quality-discount wedge in Chapter 3 |
| `target_chapter` | Ch2 (correctness wedge motivation); referenced again in Ch3 estimand justification |

## Research unit and screening

| Screen | Value |
|---|---|
| `research_unit` | `developer` |
| `unit_alignment` | `mismatch` |
| `psychology_adjacent` | `borderline` |

**Note.** Google engineer self-reports; use as framing statement for the quality-productivity coupling only, not as evidence for repository-level productivity claims. Self-report methodology places the paper at the psychology-adjacent border.

## Decision rationale

The citation signal is thin (29 total, 1 influential) and this is the only Block B anchor where the numeric signal argues against inclusion. Three considerations argue for inclusion despite that: (1) the paper is only three years old and the FSE 2022 productivity cohort is still building citations, (2) the venue (CORE A* conference) and authorship (Nagappan and Zimmermann are established Microsoft Research alumni) carry provenance weight independent of citation count, and (3) the thesis role is unique. No other Block B reference states the quality-as-productivity-input coupling this cleanly at industrial scale in the AI-code era. Rejecting the paper would leave the quality-discount wedge without a clean motivational citation, which is a larger defensibility risk than including a thinly cited but well-argued paper. The weakness is documented here rather than concealed.

**Decision:** Include in Track 2.

title: The race between man and machine: Implications of technology for growth, factor shares, and employment
rationale_md:
# T2-A01 — Acemoglu & Restrepo (2018), "The race between man and machine: Implications of technology for growth, factor shares, and employment"

**Status:** Marked for Track 2 inclusion (retrospective decision markdown, 2026-09-02). Row already present in `01b_identification_track2_anchors.csv`.

## Bibliographic entry

Acemoglu, D., & Restrepo, P. (2018). The race between man and machine: Implications of technology for growth, factor shares, and employment. *American Economic Review*, *108*(6), 1488-1542. https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20160696

**DOI:** `10.1257/aer.20160696`

## Quality signals (retrieved 2026-09-02)

| Signal | Value |
|---|---|
| Semantic Scholar total citations | 2,526 |
| Semantic Scholar influential citations | 163 |
| Venue | American Economic Review |
| Venue tier | Flagship general-interest economics journal |
| SJR quartile | Q1 |

## Why it matters for the correctness wedge

Acemoglu and Restrepo formalise the task-based model of automation and labour, distinguishing displacement effects (routine tasks replaced by capital) from reinstatement effects (new non-routine tasks that raise labour demand). For the thesis, this is the theoretical scaffold that says automation of routine coding tasks (the effect Copilot targets) does not translate cleanly into aggregate productivity gain, because it intensifies demand on the residual non-routine verification tasks that remain human. The correctness wedge is the specific instance where verification is the non-routine task now bearing the load.

## Fit vs Ch2 sections

- Primary theoretical anchor for §2.4.2 (task-based labour) in the Ch2 theory synthesis.
- Provides the displacement-versus-reinstatement mechanism that the thesis inverts to argue that Copilot-generated code shifts task load onto review and verification rather than eliminating labour requirements.
- Elite venue and citation profile mean the anchor is unassailable at viva on either provenance or currency grounds.

## Track 2 categorisation (recorded)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| `anchor_id` | `T2-A01` |
| `category` | `theory` |
| `register` | `valid_carryover` |
| `source_method` | `purposive_selection` |
| `discovery_provenance` | Section 2 (Valid References) of thesis-pivot-references-gmnb.docx |
| `target_chapter` | Ch2 (§2.4.2 task-based labour) |

## Decision rationale

Elite signals across every axis: AER is the flagship general-interest economics journal (Q1), 2,526 total citations with 163 influential, and Acemoglu is the most-cited living labour economist. The paper's role as the primary task-based-labour anchor for §2.4.2 is not substitutable within the current theory synthesis. Included as valid carryover; no defensibility risk on this row.

**Decision:** Include in Track 2 (carryover confirmed).

title: Learning curves in manufacturing
rationale_md:
# T2-A02 — Argote & Epple (1990), "Learning curves in manufacturing"

**Status:** Marked for Track 2 inclusion (retrospective decision markdown, 2026-09-02). Row already present in `01b_identification_track2_anchors.csv`.

## Bibliographic entry

Argote, L., & Epple, D. (1990). Learning curves in manufacturing. *Science*, *247*(4945), 920-924. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.247.4945.920

**DOI:** `10.1126/science.247.4945.920`

## Quality signals (retrieved 2026-09-02)

| Signal | Value |
|---|---|
| Semantic Scholar total citations | 1,347 |
| Semantic Scholar influential citations | 61 |
| Venue | Science |
| Venue tier | Elite general-science journal |
| SJR quartile | Q1 |

## Why it matters for the correctness wedge

Argote and Epple formalise organisational learning curves in manufacturing, showing that productivity improvements from cumulative experience are heterogeneous, decay over time, and often fail to transfer between plants. For the thesis, this is the organisational-learning bridge in §2.4: the mechanism by which teams accumulate correctness-relevant knowledge (idioms, review conventions, informal quality norms) is subject to the same heterogeneity and decay dynamics. Copilot's productivity claim presumes seamless integration into the team's learning stock; the paper supplies the reference against which that presumption is measured.

## Fit vs Ch2 sections

- Bridging anchor for §2.4 organisational-learning synthesis, sitting between IT productivity (§2.4.1) and absorptive capacity (§2.4.3).
- Supports the diffusion-and-assimilation claim that productivity effects from a new tool are neither instantaneous nor uniform across teams.
- Provides the classical-manufacturing precedent that repository-level learning is a legitimate analytical unit for software work.

## Track 2 categorisation (recorded)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| `anchor_id` | `T2-A02` |
| `category` | `theory` |
| `register` | `valid_carryover` |
| `source_method` | `purposive_selection` |
| `discovery_provenance` | Section 2 (Valid References) of thesis-pivot-references-gmnb.docx |
| `target_chapter` | Ch2 (§2.4 organisational learning bridge) |

## Decision rationale

Science publication with 1,347 citations and 61 influential is elite-tier for a 35-year-old empirical piece. The paper's role as the organisational-learning bridge in §2.4 is not substitutable; removing it would leave §2.4.1 and §2.4.3 without an explicit learning-dynamics link. Included as valid carryover.

**Decision:** Include in Track 2 (carryover confirmed).

**Status:** Marked for Track 2 inclusion (retrospective decision markdown, 2026-09-02). Row already present in `01b_identification_track2_anchors.csv`.

Autor, D. H., Levy, F., & Murnane, R. J. (2003). The skill content of recent technological change: An empirical exploration. *The Quarterly Journal of Economics*, *118*(4), 1279-1333. https://doi.org/10.1162/003355303322552801

## Why it matters for the correctness wedge

Autor, Levy and Murnane introduce the routine-versus-non-routine task classification that underpins modern task-based labour economics. Their empirical claim is that computerisation substitutes for routine cognitive and manual tasks while complementing non-routine analytic and interactive tasks. For the thesis, this is the joint theoretical anchor with Acemoglu and Restrepo (2018): routine code generation is precisely the task class Copilot targets, and the paper supplies the empirical warrant for reasoning about what non-routine tasks remain (verification, review, integration) as the residual load.

## Fit vs Ch2 sections

- Joint anchor with T2-A01 (Acemoglu and Restrepo 2018) for §2.4.2 task-based labour.
- Supplies the routine-versus-non-routine construct that the thesis inherits when arguing that Copilot displaces routine coding but intensifies demand on residual non-routine review work.
- Referenced universally in the task-based-labour literature, making omission indefensible.

## Track 2 categorisation (recorded)

| `discovery_provenance` | Section 2 (Valid References) of thesis-pivot-references-gmnb.docx |
| `target_chapter` | Ch2 (§2.4.2 task-based labour) |

## Decision rationale

The zero S2 citation count is an indexing artefact, not a quality signal: S2 does not index pre-2005 MIT Press QJE DOIs. Google Scholar counts for this paper exceed 10,000. QJE is a top-five general-interest economics journal and the routine-versus-non-routine construct is canonical in labour economics. Omitting the joint task-based-labour anchor would be indefensible at viva. Included as valid carryover; the S2 gap is documented in this decision markdown so the audit trail is honest.

**Decision:** Include in Track 2 (carryover confirmed).
